e-21137.worked_solution:
To find the values of $c_1$ and $c_2$, we substitute $t=0$ in the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}3{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}-{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}3{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}=7 \\ {c}_{1}-{c}_{2}=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the second equation by $2$ and adding the result to the first equation, we get

$$
5c_1= 5 
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
c_1 = 1.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
1 - c_2 = -1
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
c_2 = 2.
$$

 
Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =1\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+2\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

e-5609.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Given the Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues of the Corresponding Matrix
e-5609.problem:
Let $\lambda_1=3$ and $\lambda_2=-2$ be eigenvalues of the $2\times 2$ matrix  $A$ that correspond to eigenvectors 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067494/assets/15d8764ce12b985a991ca9a0704ba037ccc29fa488a3f23ee643688ceebae60c.png) 
Given that the position of a particle at time $t$ seconds is given by the vector $\mathbf{x}(t)$ and that $\mathbf{x}(t)$ is the solution to the initial value problem
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067494/assets/88cd1c87501899a5d6b49ce3fd1678fe9485300a2da638fb496f2c80b298ea86.png)
find the position of the particle after $2$ seconds.
e-5609.worked_solution:
Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)
$$

where $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues ${\color{red}\lambda_1}, {\color{blue}\lambda_2}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2},$ the formula for the general solution is

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{red}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{blue}\lambda_2} t}, \qquad c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the values of $c_1$ and $c_2,$ we substitute $t=0$ into the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}-11 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}-11 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}6{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ -2{c}_{1}-3{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-11 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}6{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=-11 \\ -2{c}_{1}-3{c}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first equation by $3$ and adding the result to the second equation, we get

$$
16c_1 = -32
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
c_1=-2.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
-2\cdot(-2) -3c_2 = 1
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
c_2=1.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution for the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =-2\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+1\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-12 \\ 4\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate $\mathbf x(2)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2) & =[\begin{aligned}-12 \\ 4\end{aligned}]{e}^{3\cdot 2}+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2\cdot 2} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-12{e}^{6}+{e}^{-4} \\ 4{e}^{6}-3{e}^{-4}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

e-5608.worked_solution:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067494/assets/4790200622ff45c885147ca0c897eefcbb4bdcefe10d67b8960cc167c3b2cccf.png)

- We are given that the eigenvalues are

$$
\lambda_1= 2
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\lambda_2= -3.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For $\lambda_1 =2,$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067494/assets/10bbcec99a48d331c21836dc104a1db2db241e50a534baf0db23c138168c5663.png)
So, we get an eigenvector 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067494/assets/c2bff2faa79d780c5f89b28e72468c84a388d50e8c566b80e5d5677f90a5e3af.png)

- For $\lambda_2 =-3,$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067494/assets/704493d5ac4f48c88a9c521c4e43c41acfd80b6d6959237944fbc0d638e6012f.png)
So, we get an eigenvector 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067494/assets/a77312d93a804e69dabb70aff5bc7bbf9798781c728dfc50fff1440da86b5b5c.png)

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 6\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the values of $c_1$ and $c_2,$ we substitute $t=0$ in the general solution and use the initial values:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 6\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}+6{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=5 \\ {c}_{1}+6{c}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the first equation from the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5{c}_{2}=-5\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $c_2 = -1$ into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}-1=5\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=6.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =6[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 6\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Given the General Solution
content.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

given that the general solution to our differential equation is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The solution to the initial value problem is

| $x(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} |  | $\,\,{e}^{t}+\,\,$ |  | {{field-2}} |  | $\,\,{e}^{-t}.$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} |  |  | {{field-4}} |  |  |  |  |
content.worked_solution:
To find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$, we substitute $t=0$ in the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}-{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=4 \\ {c}_{1}-{c}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the equations, we get

$$
2{c}_{1}=4\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=2.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
2+{c}_{2}=4\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=2.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix with eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ corresponding to the eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ respectively, where

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Given that the position of a particle at time $t$ seconds is given by the vector $x(t),$ and that $x(t)$ is the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}],
$$

find the position of the particle at $t=7$ seconds.
after.worked_solution:
Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),
$$

where $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2},$ the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$, we substitute $t=0$ into the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-{c}_{1}+4{c}_{2} \\ -{c}_{1}+3{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-{c}_{1}+4{c}_{2}=6 \\ -{c}_{1}+3{c}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the second equation by $-1$ and adding the result to the first equation, we get

$$
{c}_{2}=6.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-{c}_{1}+4\cdot 6=6\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=18.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =18\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+6\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-18 \\ -18\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+[\begin{aligned}24 \\ 18\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate $x(7)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(7) & =[\begin{aligned}-18 \\ -18\end{aligned}]{e}^{4\cdot 7}+[\begin{aligned}24 \\ 18\end{aligned}]{e}^{-7} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-18 \\ -18\end{aligned}]{e}^{28}+[\begin{aligned}24 \\ 18\end{aligned}]{e}^{-7} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-18{e}^{28}+24{e}^{-7} \\ -18{e}^{28}+18{e}^{-7}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6

Let A be a 2×2 matrix with eigenvalues λ1=4 and λ2=−1 corresponding to the eigenvectors v1 and v2 respectively, where

v1=[−1−1],v2=[43]. Given that the position of a particle at time t seconds is given by the vector x(t), and that x(t) is the solution to the initial value problem x′(t)=Ax(t),x(0)=[60], find the position of the particle at t=7 seconds.

a
[−18e28+24e−7−18e28+18e−7]
b
[−18e7+24e−7−18e7+18e−7]
c
[6e28+18e−70]
d
[18e28+24e−7−6e28+18e−7]
e
[−12e28+28e−7−18e28+16e−7]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form x′(t)=Ax(t), where A has two distinct eigenvalues λ1,λ2 with corresponding eigenvectors v1 and v2, the formula for the general solution is x(t)=c1v1eλ1t+c2v2eλ2t,c1,c2∈R.

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

x(t)=c1[−1−1]e4t+c2[43]e−t,c1,c2∈R.

Now, to find the values of c1 and c2, we substitute t=0 into the general solution:

x(0)=[60]c1[−1−1]e0+c2[43]e0=[60][−c1+4c2−c1+3c2]=[60]

So, we have a system of linear equations {−c1+4c2=6−c1+3c2=0.

Multiplying the second equation by −1 and adding the result to the first equation, we get c2=6.

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain −c1+4⋅6=6⟹c1=18.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

x(t)=18⋅[−1−1]e4t+6⋅[43]e−t=[−18−18]e4t+[2418]e−t.

Finally, we calculate x(7):

x(7)=[−18−18]e4⋅7+[2418]e−7=[−18−18]e28+[2418]e−7=[−18e28+24e−7−18e28+18e−7]

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Given the Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues of the Corresponding Matrix
content.problem:
Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix with eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ corresponding to the eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ respectively, where

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Given that the position of a particle at time $t$ seconds is given by the vector $x(t),$ and that $x(t)$ is the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}],
$$

find the position of the particle at $t=7$ seconds.
content.worked_solution:
Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),
$$

where $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2},$ the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$, we substitute $t=0$ into the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-{c}_{1}+4{c}_{2} \\ -{c}_{1}+3{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-{c}_{1}+4{c}_{2}=6 \\ -{c}_{1}+3{c}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the second equation by $-1$ and adding the result to the first equation, we get

$$
{c}_{2}=6.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-{c}_{1}+4\cdot 6=6\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=18.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =18\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+6\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-18 \\ -18\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+[\begin{aligned}24 \\ 18\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate $x(7)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(7) & =[\begin{aligned}-18 \\ -18\end{aligned}]{e}^{4\cdot 7}+[\begin{aligned}24 \\ 18\end{aligned}]{e}^{-7} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-18 \\ -18\end{aligned}]{e}^{28}+[\begin{aligned}24 \\ 18\end{aligned}]{e}^{-7} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-18{e}^{28}+24{e}^{-7} \\ -18{e}^{28}+18{e}^{-7}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Let A be a 2×2 matrix with eigenvalues λ1=−2 and λ2=3 corresponding to the eigenvectors v1 and v2 respectively, where v1=[−15],v2=[1−1]. Given that the position of a particle at time t seconds is given by the vector x(t), and that x(t) is the solution to the initial value problem x′(t)=Ax(t),x(0)=[31], find the position of the particle at t=2 seconds.

a
[3e−4+4e6e−4−4e6]
b
[−e−4+4e65e−4−4e6]
c
[−e−45e6]
d
[3e6−4e−4+e6]
e
[e−4+3e6−e−4]
Submit

decision.explanation: Write x(t)=c_1v_1e^{-2t}+c_2v_2e^{3t}. The initial condition gives -c_1+c_2=3 and 5c_1-c_2=1. Adding yields c_1=1, then c_2=4. Thus x(2)=[-e^{-4}+4e^6,5e^{-4}-4e^6]^T, matching option b.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix with eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ corresponding to the eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ respectively, where

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Given that the position of a particle at time $t$ seconds is given by the vector $x(t),$ and that $x(t)$ is the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

find the position of the particle at $t=2$ seconds.
after.worked_solution:
Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),
$$

where $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2},$ the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$, we substitute $t=0$ into the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2(0)}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3(0)} & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 5{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=3 \\ 5{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the equations, we get

$$
4{c}_{1}=4\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=1.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-1+{c}_{2}=3\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=4.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =1[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+4[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate $x(2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2) & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2(2)}+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]{e}^{3(2)} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-4}+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]{e}^{6} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{-4}+4{e}^{6} \\ 5{e}^{-4}-4{e}^{6}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form x′(t)=Ax(t), where A has two distinct eigenvalues λ1,λ2 with corresponding eigenvectors v1 and v2, the formula for the general solution is x(t)=c1v1eλ1t+c2v2eλ2t,c1,c2∈R.

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is x(t)=c1v1eλ1t+c2v2eλ2t=c1[−15]e−2t+c2[1−1]e3t,c1,c2∈R.

Now, to find the values of c1 and c2, we substitute t=0 into the general solution:

x(0)=[31]c1[−15]e−2(0)+c2[1−1]e3(0)=[31]c1[−15]+c2[1−1]=[31][−c1+c25c1−c2]=[31]

So, we have a system of linear equations {−c1+c2=35c1−c2=1.

Adding the equations, we get 4c1=4⟹c1=1. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain −1+c2=3⟹c2=4.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is x(t)=1[−15]e−2t+4[1−1]e3t=[−15]e−2t+[4−4]e3t.

Finally, we calculate x(2): x(2)=[−15]e−2(2)+[4−4]e3(2)=[−15]e−4+[4−4]e6=[−e−4+4e65e−4−4e6]

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms c_1=1 and c_2=4 from -c_1+c_2=3 and 5c_1-c_2=1. Therefore x(2)=[-e^{-4}+4e^6,5e^{-4}-4e^6]^T, matching option b. The deliberately submitted option c is incorrect.

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Given the Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues of the Corresponding Matrix
content.problem:
Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix with eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ corresponding to the eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ respectively, where

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Given that the position of a particle at time $t$ seconds is given by the vector $x(t),$ and that $x(t)$ is the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

find the position of the particle at $t=2$ seconds.
content.worked_solution:
Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),
$$

where $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2},$ the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$, we substitute $t=0$ into the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2(0)}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3(0)} & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 5{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=3 \\ 5{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the equations, we get

$$
4{c}_{1}=4\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=1.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-1+{c}_{2}=3\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=4.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =1[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+4[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate $x(2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2) & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2(2)}+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]{e}^{3(2)} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-4}+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]{e}^{6} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{-4}+4{e}^{6} \\ 5{e}^{-4}-4{e}^{6}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Let A be a 2×2 matrix with eigenvalues λ1=0 and λ2=2 corresponding to the eigenvectors v1 and v2 respectively, where

v1=[10],v2=[22]. Given that the position of a particle at time t seconds is given by the vector x(t), and that x(t) is the solution to the initial value problem x′(t)=Ax(t),x(0)=[51], find the position of the particle at t=5 seconds.

a
 [4+e5e5]
b
 [4+e10e10]
c
 [5+e101+e10]
d
 [4+e100]
e
 [4+e2e2]
Submit

decision.explanation: The solution is x(t)=c_1[1,0]^T+c_2[2,2]^T e^{2t}. At t=0, 2c_2=1 and c_1+2c_2=5, so c_2=1/2 and c_1=4. Hence x(5)=[4+e^{10},e^{10}]^T, matching option b.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix with eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2$ corresponding to the eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ respectively, where

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Given that the position of a particle at time $t$ seconds is given by the vector $x(t),$ and that $x(t)$ is the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

find the position of the particle at $t=5$ seconds.
after.worked_solution:
Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),
$$

where $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2},$ the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$, we substitute $t=0$ into the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2} \\ 2{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}=5 \\ 2{c}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{c}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{c}_{1}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}=5\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=4.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution for the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =4\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate $x(5)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(5) & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2\cdot 5} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{10} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4+{e}^{10} \\ {e}^{10}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Let A be a 2×2 matrix with eigenvalues λ1=0 and λ2=2 corresponding to the eigenvectors v1 and v2 respectively, where

v1=[10],v2=[22]. Given that the position of a particle at time t seconds is given by the vector x(t), and that x(t) is the solution to the initial value problem x′(t)=Ax(t),x(0)=[51], find the position of the particle at t=5 seconds.

a
 [4+e5e5]
b
 [4+e10e10]
c
 [5+e101+e10]
d
 [4+e100]
e
 [4+e2e2]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form x′(t)=Ax(t), where A has two distinct eigenvalues λ1,λ2 with corresponding eigenvectors v1 and v2, the formula for the general solution is x(t)=c1v1eλ1t+c2v2eλ2t,c1,c2∈R.

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

x(t)=c1v1eλ1t+c2v2eλ2t=c1[10]e0+c2[22]e2t=c1[10]+c2[22]e2t,c1,c2∈R.

Now, to find the values of c1 and c2, we substitute t=0 into the general solution:

x(0)=[51]c1[10]+c2[22]e0=[51][c1+2c22c2]=[51]

So, we have a system of linear equations {c1+2c2=52c2=1.

From the second equation, we obtain c2=12. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain c1+2⋅12=5⟹c1=4.

Therefore, the solution for the initial value problem is

x(t)=4⋅[10]+12⋅[22]e2t=[40]+[11]e2t.

Finally, we calculate x(5):

x(5)=[40]+[11]e2⋅5=[40]+[11]e10=[4+e10e10]

content.problem:
Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix with eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2$ corresponding to the eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ respectively, where

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Given that the position of a particle at time $t$ seconds is given by the vector $x(t),$ and that $x(t)$ is the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

find the position of the particle at $t=5$ seconds.
content.worked_solution:
Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),
$$

where $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2},$ the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$, we substitute $t=0$ into the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2} \\ 2{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}=5 \\ 2{c}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{c}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{c}_{1}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}=5\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=4.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution for the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =4\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate $x(5)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(5) & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2\cdot 5} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{10} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4+{e}^{10} \\ {e}^{10}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

v1=[41],v2=[10]. Solve the following initial value problem: x′(t)=Ax(t),x(0)=[43]

a
x(t)=[13]e8t+[−80]e2t
b
x(t)=[123]e4t+[−280]e2t
c
x(t)=[03]e−3t+[−40]e2t
d
x(t)=[23]e3t+[−180]e2t
e
x(t)=[123]e3t+[−80]e2t
Submit

decision.explanation: The general solution is x(t)=c_1[4,1]^T e^{3t}+c_2[1,0]^T e^{2t}. The initial condition gives c_1=3 and 4c_1+c_2=4, so c_2=-8. This yields option e and satisfies x(0)=[4,3]^T.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix with eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2$ corresponding to the eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ respectively, where

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Solve the following initial value problem:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$
after.worked_solution:
Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),
$$

where $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2},$ the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$, we substitute $t=0$ in the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=4 \\ {c}_{1}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{c}_{1}=3.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
4\cdot 3+{c}_{2}=4\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=-8.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution for the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =3\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+(-8)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Let A be a 2×2 matrix with eigenvalues λ1=3 and λ2=2 corresponding to the eigenvectors v1 and v2 respectively, where

v1=[41],v2=[10]. Solve the following initial value problem: x′(t)=Ax(t),x(0)=[43]

a
x(t)=[13]e8t+[−80]e2t
b
x(t)=[123]e4t+[−280]e2t
c
x(t)=[03]e−3t+[−40]e2t
d
x(t)=[23]e3t+[−180]e2t
e
x(t)=[123]e3t+[−80]e2t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form x′(t)=Ax(t), where A has two distinct eigenvalues λ1,λ2 with corresponding eigenvectors v1 and v2, the formula for the general solution is x(t)=c1v1eλ1t+c2v2eλ2t,c1,c2∈R.

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

x(t)=c1[41]e3t+c2[10]e2t,c1,c2∈R.

Now, to find the values of c1 and c2, we substitute t=0 in the general solution:

x(0)=[43]c1[41]e0+c2[10]e0=[43][4c1+c2c1]=[43]

So, we have a system of linear equations {4c1+c2=4c1=3. From the second equation, we obtain c1=3. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 4⋅3+c2=4⟹c2=−8.

Therefore, the solution for the initial value problem is

x(t)=3⋅[41]e3t+(−8)⋅[10]e2t=[123]e3t+[−80]e2t.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms c_1=3 and c_2=-8. Thus option e uses the correct eigenvalue exponents and gives x(0)=[12-8,3]^T=[4,3]^T. The deliberately submitted option b is incorrect.

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Given the Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues of the Corresponding Matrix
content.problem:
Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix with eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2$ corresponding to the eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ respectively, where

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Solve the following initial value problem:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$
content.worked_solution:
Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),
$$

where $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2},$ the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$, we substitute $t=0$ in the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=4 \\ {c}_{1}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{c}_{1}=3.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
4\cdot 3+{c}_{2}=4\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=-8.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution for the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =3\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+(-8)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

before.problem:
Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix with eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ corresponding to the eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ respectively, where

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Solve the following initial value problem:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 10
?

Let A be a 2×2 matrix with eigenvalues λ1=1 and λ2=−1 corresponding to the eigenvectors v1 and v2 respectively, where

v1=[1−2],v2=[22]. Solve the following initial value problem: x′(t)=Ax(t),x(0)=[3−3]

a
 x(t)=[2−4]e−t+[11]et
b
 x(t)=[2−5]et+[12]e−t
c
 x(t)=[2−4]et+[11]e−t
d
 x(t)=[2−4]et
e
 x(t)=[2−4]et+[22]e−t
Submit

decision.explanation: Write x(t)=c_1v_1e^t+c_2v_2e^{-t}. The initial condition gives c_1+2c_2=3 and -2c_1+2c_2=-3, so c_1=2 and c_2=1/2. Therefore x(t)=[2,-4]^T e^t+[1,1]^T e^{-t}, matching option c.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix with eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ corresponding to the eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ respectively, where

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Solve the following initial value problem:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}]
$$
after.worked_solution:
Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),
$$

where $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2},$ the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$, we substitute $t=0$ in the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2} \\ -2{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}=3 \\ -2{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first equation by $2$ and adding the result to the second equation, we get

$$
6{c}_{2}=3\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{c}_{1}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}=3\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=2.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Let A be a 2×2 matrix with eigenvalues λ1=1 and λ2=−1 corresponding to the eigenvectors v1 and v2 respectively, where

v1=[1−2],v2=[22]. Solve the following initial value problem: x′(t)=Ax(t),x(0)=[3−3]

a
 x(t)=[2−4]e−t+[11]et
b
 x(t)=[2−5]et+[12]e−t
c
 x(t)=[2−4]et+[11]e−t
d
 x(t)=[2−4]et
e
 x(t)=[2−4]et+[22]e−t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form x′(t)=Ax(t), where A has two distinct eigenvalues λ1,λ2 with corresponding eigenvectors v1 and v2, the formula for the general solution is x(t)=c1v1eλ1t+c2v2eλ2t,c1,c2∈R.

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

x(t)=c1[1−2]et+c2[22]e−t,c1,c2∈R.

Now, to find the values of c1 and c2, we substitute t=0 in the general solution:

x(0)=[3−3]c1[1−2]e0+c2[22]e0=[3−3][c1+2c2−2c1+2c2]=[3−3]

So, we have a system of linear equations {c1+2c2=3−2c1+2c2=−3. Multiplying the first equation by 2 and adding the result to the second equation, we get 6c2=3⟹c2=12.

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain c1+2⋅12=3⟹c1=2.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is x(t)=2⋅[1−2]et+12⋅[22]e−t=[2−4]et+[11]e−t.

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Given the Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues of the Corresponding Matrix
content.problem:
Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix with eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ corresponding to the eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ respectively, where

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Solve the following initial value problem:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}]
$$
content.worked_solution:
Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),
$$

where $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2},$ the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$, we substitute $t=0$ in the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2} \\ -2{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}=3 \\ -2{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first equation by $2$ and adding the result to the second equation, we get

$$
6{c}_{2}=3\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{c}_{1}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}=3\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=2.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

before.name: Question 11
before.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-3{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-4{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t),\end{aligned}\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$*

Question 11
?

Find the solution to the initial value problem {x1′(t)=−3x1(t)+x2(t)x2′(t)=−4x1(t)+2x2(t),x(0)=[2−1].

Hint: The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are λ1=1 and λ2=−2.

a
x(t)=[3−1]e4t−[10]e−t
b
x(t)=2[3−1]e4t−4[10]e−t
c
x(t)=−2[14]et+4[11]e−2t
d
x(t)=[14]et+[11]e−2t
e
x(t)=−[14]et+3[11]e−2t
Submit

decision.explanation: For A=[-3,1;-4,2], A[1,4]^T=[1,4]^T and A[1,1]^T=-2[1,1]^T. Thus x(t)=c_1[1,4]^T e^t+c_2[1,1]^T e^{-2t}. The initial condition gives c_1+c_2=2 and 4c_1+c_2=-1, hence c_1=-1 and c_2=3, matching option e.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-3{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-4{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t),\end{aligned}\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$*
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ for the given system:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A.$

- We are given that the eigenvalues are

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=1\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1/4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -4 & 4\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2(0)} & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ 4{c}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=2 \\ 4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the first equation from the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{c}_{1}=-3\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${c}_{1}=-1$ into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}-1+{c}_{2}=2\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem for a Linear System of Differential Equations
content.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-3{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-4{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t),\end{aligned}\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$*
content.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ for the given system:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A.$

- We are given that the eigenvalues are

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=1\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1/4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -4 & 4\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2(0)} & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ 4{c}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=2 \\ 4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the first equation from the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{c}_{1}=-3\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${c}_{1}=-1$ into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}-1+{c}_{2}=2\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}
$$

a
x(t)=−72[21]et+12[01]e3t
b
x(t)=12[21]et−72[01]e3t
c

e

decision.explanation: For A=[1,0;-1,3], the eigenvectors [2,1]^T and [0,1]^T have eigenvalues 1 and 3. Thus x(t)=c_1[2,1]^T e^t+c_2[0,1]^T e^{3t}. The initial condition gives 2c_1=1 and c_1+c_2=-3, so c_1=1/2 and c_2=-7/2, matching option b.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t),\end{aligned}\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ for the given system:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A.$

- Since $A$ is lower-triangular, the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=1\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=3.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{1}+{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}2{c}_{1}=1 \\ {c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get ${c}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting into the second equation, we obtain ${c}_{2}=-\frac{7}{2}.$ 

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}-\frac{7}{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}
$$

  • Since A is lower-triangular, the eigenvalues are λ1=1andλ2=3.

  • Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

    • For λ1=1, we get A−λ1I=[00−12]∼[1−200]. So, we get an eigenvector v1=[21].

    • For λ2=3, we get A−λ2I=[−20−10]∼[1000]. So, we get an eigenvector v2=[01].

x(t)=c1v1eλ1t+c2v2eλ2t=c1[21]et+c2[01]e3t,c1,c2∈R

x(0)=[1−3]c1[21]e0+c2[01]e0=[1−3][2c1c1+c2]=[1−3]

So, we have a system of linear equations {2c1=1c1+c2=−3.

From the first equation, we get c1=12. Substituting into the second equation, we obtain c2=−72.

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

x(t)=12[21]et−72[01]e3t

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem for a Linear System of Differential Equations
content.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t),\end{aligned}\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ for the given system:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A.$

- Since $A$ is lower-triangular, the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=1\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=3.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{1}+{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}2{c}_{1}=1 \\ {c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get ${c}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting into the second equation, we obtain ${c}_{2}=-\frac{7}{2}.$ 

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}-\frac{7}{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13
?

Find the solution to the initial value problem {x1′(t)=5x1(t)−3x2(t)x2′(t)=2x2(t),x(0)=[−53].

a
x(t)=8[01]e5t+3[−11]e2t
b
x(t)=−4[10]e3t+2[11]e4t
c
x(t)=−3[10]e5t−8[11]e2t
d
x(t)=−3[10]e5t+8[11]e2t
e
x(t)=−8[10]e5t+3[11]e2t
Submit

decision.explanation: Since x_2'=2x_2 and x_2(0)=3, x_2(t)=3e^{2t}. Substituting into the first equation gives x_1(t)=Ce^{5t}+3e^{2t}; x_1(0)=-5 implies C=-8. This is option e.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=5{x}_{1}(t)-3{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=2{x}_{2}(t),\end{aligned}\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ for the given system:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A.$

First, we write down the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ for the given system:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A.$

- Since $A$ is upper-triangular, the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=2.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=-5 \\ {c}_{2}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${c}_{2}=3.$ Substituting into the first equation, we obtain ${c}_{1}=-8.$ 

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =-8[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}+3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem for a Linear System of Differential Equations
content.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=5{x}_{1}(t)-3{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=2{x}_{2}(t),\end{aligned}\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ for the given system:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A.$

First, we write down the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ for the given system:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A.$

- Since $A$ is upper-triangular, the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=2.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=-5 \\ {c}_{2}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${c}_{2}=3.$ Substituting into the first equation, we obtain ${c}_{1}=-8.$ 

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =-8[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}+3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

Find the solution to the initial value problem {x1′(t)=x1(t)−x2(t)x2′(t)=−2x1(t)+2x2(t),x(1)=[−2e4e4].

Hint: The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are λ1=3 and λ2=0.

a
x(t)=2e[−12]e3t+e3[1−1]
b
x(t)=2[−12]e−3t−3[11]
c
x(t)=e[−12]e3t−e4[11]
d
x(t)=−2e2[−12]e3t−3e[11]
e
x(t)=2e[1−2]e2t−3e4[11]
Submit

decision.explanation: The vectors [-1,2]^T and [1,1]^T have eigenvalues 3 and 0, so x(t)=c_1[-1,2]^T e^{3t}+c_2[1,1]^T. At t=1, -c_1e^3+c_2=-2e^4 and 2c_1e^3+c_2=e^4. Subtracting gives c_1=e, then c_2=-e^4. This matches option c.

after.name: Question 14
after.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-2{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned},\,x(1)=[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{4} \\ {e}^{4}\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=0.$*
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ for the given system:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A.$

- We are given that the eigenvalues are

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=0.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1/2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ Substituting $t=1$ into the general solution, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(1) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4} \\ {e}^{4}\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{3}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{4} \\ {e}^{4}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-{e}^{3}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 2{e}^{3}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{4} \\ {e}^{4}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-{e}^{3}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=-2{e}^{4} \\ 2{e}^{3}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}={e}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3}{c}_{1}=3{e}^{4}\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=e.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${c}_{1}=e$ into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{e}^{3}(e)+{c}_{2}={e}^{4}\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=-{e}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =e[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}-{e}^{4}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hint: The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are λ1=3 and λ2=0.

EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix differential equation x′(t)=Ax(t) for the given system:

[x1′(t)x2′(t)]=[1−1−22][x1(t)x2(t)]

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix A.

  • We are given that the eigenvalues are λ1=3andλ2=0.

  • Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

    • For λ1=3, we get A−λ1I=[−2−1−2−1]∼[11/200]. So, we get an eigenvector v1=[−12].

    • For λ2=0, we get A−λ2I=[1−1−22]∼[1−100]. So, we get an eigenvector v2=[11].

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations:

x(t)=c1v1eλ1t+c2v2eλ2t=c1[−12]e3t+c2[11]e0=c1[−12]e3t+c2[11],c1,c2∈R.

Next, we find the values of c1 and c2. Substituting t=1 into the general solution, we get the following:

x(1)=[e4e4]c1[−12]e3+c2[11]=[−2e4e4][−e3c1+c22e3c1+c2]=[−2e4e4]

So, we have a system of linear equations {−e3c1+c2=−2e42e3c1+c2=e4. Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get

3e3c1=3e4⟹c1=e.

Substituting c1=e into the second equation, we obtain

2e3(e)+c2=e4⟹c2=−e4.

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

x(t)=e[−12]e3t−e4[11]

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem for a Linear System of Differential Equations
content.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-2{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned},\,x(1)=[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{4} \\ {e}^{4}\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=0.$*
content.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ for the given system:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A.$

- We are given that the eigenvalues are

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=0.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1/2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =e[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}-{e}^{4}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

Find the solution to the following initial value problem. {x1′(t)=4x1(t)+x2(t)x2′(t)=−x2(t),x(0)=[−110]

a
x(t)=2[10]e4t+3[−15]e−t
b
x(t)=[−13]e2t+[07]et
c
x(t)=2[10]e4t−[−15]e−t

x(t)=−[−13]e2t+2[07]et
e

decision.explanation: The second equation gives x_2(t)=10e^{-t}. Then x_1'=4x_1+10e^{-t} has solution x_1(t)=Ce^{4t}-2e^{-t}. Since x_1(0)=-1, C=1. Thus option e satisfies both equations and the initial condition.

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
Find the solution to the following initial value problem.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=4{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{2}(t),\end{aligned}\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 10\end{aligned}]
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ for the given system:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A.$

- Since $A$ is upper-triangular, the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=4\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=-1.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{4(0)}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-0} & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\ 5{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}=-1 \\ 5{c}_{2}=10.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${c}_{2}=2.$ Substituting into the first equation, we obtain ${c}_{1}=1.$ 

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+2[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations {c1−c2=−15c2=10.

From the second equation, we get c2=2. Substituting into the first equation, we obtain c1=1.

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem for a Linear System of Differential Equations
content.problem:
Find the solution to the following initial value problem.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=4{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{2}(t),\end{aligned}\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 10\end{aligned}]
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ for the given system:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A.$

- Since $A$ is upper-triangular, the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=4\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=-1.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{4(0)}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-0} & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\ 5{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}=-1 \\ 5{c}_{2}=10.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${c}_{2}=2.$ Substituting into the first equation, we obtain ${c}_{1}=1.$ 

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+2[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}
$$
